captions: This is the high-level overview of the Animate Banana pipeline, which automatically transforms static process-oriented diagrams into animated narratives.
Stage one is the Diagram Transmuter, which converts the input diagram into animation-aware diagram code.
The process begins with a static input diagram.
This input diagram is fed directly into the Diagram Transmuter.
Inside, a specialized converter agent generates an initial code representation, assigning persistent semantic identifiers to all animatable elements.
This produces an initial draft of the animation-aware diagram code.
A critic agent then evaluates the rendered code against the original diagram, providing iterative feedback to the converter to refine the code's visual and structural fidelity.
Simultaneously, a raster integrator extracts complex visual regions, such as photographs or plots, and inserts them directly into the code to preserve them without reconstruction.
The final output of this stage is the refined animation-aware diagram code.
Stage two is the Animation Planner, which designs a structured presentation and narration plan.
This stage takes the diagram, optional auxiliary context, the user-specified animation style, and the generated diagram code as inputs.
First, a parser processes the diagram code.
It abstracts away rendering details to produce a structured XML representation of the diagram's entities and relationships.
A sequencer agent then reasons over this XML to construct an initial presentation sequence, determining the grouping and traversal order of elements.
A sequence critic evaluates this plan for coverage and coherence, guiding the sequencer through iterative refinement.
This results in a validated animation sequence draft, tailored to the chosen animation style.
Next, a narration drafter generates synchronized explanatory text for each step, utilizing any available auxiliary context to enrich the descriptions.
This produces the narration-infused animation sequence, coupling visual steps with spoken explanations.
Stage three is the Diagram Animator, which synthesizes the final animated narrative.
It ingests the original diagram, the chosen animation style, the narration-infused sequence, and the diagram code.
An animation designer agent generates an initial executable animation program based on these inputs.
An animation critic evaluates the rendered frames against the source diagram, using a critic memory of past feedback to correct visual and temporal errors.
This iterative process refines the executable animation code.
Once validated, an animation exporter renders the frames into the target presentation format.
In parallel, a narration integrator uses speech synthesis to align the step-level narration with the corresponding visual states.
This ensures that the visual transitions and audio explanations are perfectly synchronized.
The final output is a styled visual narrative, ready to be deployed across multiple formats such as MP4, PDF, or PowerPoint.
The training pipeline begins with the Breast Cancer Image Dataset, providing source data for segmentation and classification workflows.
In the segmentation branch, raw ultrasonography images are extracted from the dataset.
These images enter the preprocessing stage,
where they undergo dimension scaling to 128 by 128 pixels followed by pixel normalization.
Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) then clusters pixels into superpixels to mitigate noise.
The clustered images are fed into a modified U-Net encoder-decoder network alongside ground truth masks.
Completing this training yields the trained segmentation model.
In parallel, masked images and corresponding class labels are retrieved for detection training.
A pre-trained VGG 16 model extracts deep spatial features from these masked ultrasound images.
Extracted features are processed through five fully connected dense layers with dropout and activations.
This establishes the trained detection model for classifying tumor types.
Finally, the trained components combine into the unified breast cancer detection pipelining framework.
The pipeline begins with a sequence of five hundred twelve dimensional input feature vectors.
These vectors are organized into an input feature matrix labeled F sub w, with dimensions five hundred twelve by n.
Inside the scaled dot product attention sub-block, the matrix branches through fully connected layers into key transpose, query, and value matrices.
The key transpose and query representations are multiplied together and processed by a softmax function.
This yields an n-by-n matrix of self-attention weights labeled W sub s a.
The self-attention weights are then multiplied with the value matrix.
The result feeds into the cross-walk attention sub-block as an intermediate matrix labeled H sub a.
A per-row softmax operation is then applied across the matrix columns.
Next, the softmax output is combined element-wise with a bypass connection from the original matrix F sub w.
This creates the cross-walk attention matrix labeled G, with dimensions five hundred twelve by n.
The column vectors are then aggregated through a summation operation.
Finally, the system outputs the five hundred twelve dimensional feature vector labeled f sub a.
The pipeline takes K-shot support images and a query image as inputs, referencing the aggregation, tensor shape, and path notations shown in the legend.
Both the support and query images are fed into parallel Backbone Networks for feature extraction.
In the support stream, RoI pooling is performed using the support image ground truth boxes to extract pooled feature tensors.
The query features then combine with the support branch at an aggregation operation labeled Q S A.
The aggregated output flows into the R P N, followed by RoI pooling on the query feature stream.
These pooled query representations merge with the upper support features at the aggregation module labeled Q R A.
Finally, the combined features pass into the RoI Head, generating the final detection bounding boxes on the query image.
The memory architecture is divided into User Space and Kernel Space.
In User Space, execution begins at the Database Process.
The process initiates an asynchronous write call.
This is followed by a synchronous fsync operation.
The write call routes into the Page Cache within Kernel Space and returns immediately, creating dirty pages.
The Kernel Flusher Thread periodically handles writebacks from the Page Cache.
Requests pass into the I/O Queue, while fsync waits for disk completion.
At the bottom is Persistent Storage, containing the Block Device.
Finally, enqueued operations are flushed from the I/O Queue down to the Block Device.
The training pipeline begins with three inputs: the input medical image, its corresponding ground truth mask, and generated interactive masks.
A frozen image encoder extracts visual tokens from the input image, while initial interaction simulators derive point, bounding box, and text prompts from the masks.
The system then enters an iterative interaction loop that simulates multiple consecutive refinement steps.
The initial simulated interaction prompts are processed by a learnable prompt encoder.
The extracted image tokens are combined with convolutional feedback features via element-wise addition.
A learnable mask decoder integrates these fused image features with the encoded prompts and circulates intermediate features back through a convolution layer.
Transposed convolution layers then upsample the decoded representations into predicted segmentation masks for both the ground truth and interactive targets.
The framework computes error regions by identifying discrepancies between each predicted mask and its target.
Interaction simulators place corrective prompts on these error regions and feed them back to the prompt encoder, completing the feedback loop across iterations.
Pairs of experience observations are sampled from the replay buffer.
Each sampled instance pairs raw observation frames with corresponding context parameters across different environment shifts.
The encoders map these contextual observations into a shared latent representation space.
Conditioned on the policy's actions, probabilistic transition models predict the next-state distributions.
Concurrently, reward models estimate expected scalar rewards for each latent state.
Finally, bisimulation losses align latent representation distances with the combined reward differences and Wasserstein transition distances.
The pipeline begins with the synthetic dataset preparation stage.
Fractal system parameters are sampled to construct diverse mathematical configurations.
These sampled parameters are grouped together to define distinct synthetic classes for training.
During pre-training, an image generator renders fractal images on the fly from these parameter codes.
Generated batches of fractal patterns are fed directly into the vision model.
The neural network backbone processes the batch to produce category predictions.
A loss function evaluates the predictions against the synthetic target labels.
Gradients are backpropagated to update the backbone weights throughout pre-training.
For downstream evaluation, real-world image recognition datasets are introduced.
The pre-trained model is fine-tuned to achieve competitive performance across these real-world tasks.
The pipeline begins with the training dataset, containing samples with fully observed, non-missing attributes.
These samples are used to train the treatment effect estimation model, fitting the outcome predictors.
The performance of the estimator is periodically evaluated on a hold-out test set.
Meanwhile, unlabeled candidate samples with missing confounding attributes are maintained in the data pool.
A confounder acquisition strategy evaluates the pool, selecting instances based on covariate balancing or outcome estimation error.
The chosen batch forms the query set of prioritized samples.
The feature value collector retrieves the missing confounding values, adding the newly completed samples back into the training set for the next iteration.
The pipeline begins by retrieving clinical notes for Alzheimer's disease patients from the Clinical Data Repository.
The records are filtered using the rule-based NLP-PIER information extraction system.
This filtering generates a dataset of lifestyle-related sentences with automatically assigned weak labels.
The weakly labeled corpus is then used to fine-tune a suite of BERT-based sentence classifiers.
The models include Bio-Clinical BERT,
UMLS BERT,
PubMedBERT trained solely on abstracts,
PubMedBERT trained on abstracts and full text,
BioBERT,
and the standard uncased BERT base model.
The classifiers predict risk factors across two case studies, identifying excessive diet...
...and physical activity levels.
Finally, all models are tested and evaluated against a manually annotated Gold Standard Corpus.
